title: Paralympic Athletes
summary: How the Paralympic Games grew from a 1948 contest for injured soldiers into a world event where elite athletes with disabilities compete in sports such as wheelchair basketball and goalball.
poll: The Paralympic Games are just as exciting to watch as the Olympic Games.

versions.title: Para Athletes
versions.text:
Look at the track. A man zooms by. He is in a wheelchair. A girl runs on a blade. It is made of steel. A blind man runs with a guide. Wow! They are fast. They are at the Paralympic Games.

These Games are for top athletes. Each one has a disability. The Games come once in four years. They are held in the same town as the Olympics.

It all began in 1948. A man in England set up games. He was a doctor. The games were for men hurt in a war. Some could not walk. They shot with bows from their chairs. In 1960, the first real Games were held in Rome.

There are lots of sports. Some teams play ball in wheelchairs. Some swim. In goalball, the ball has bells in it. The teams hear it roll.

A blind man and a guide hold a short cord. They run side by side. The guide calls out the turns. If they win, the guide gets a medal, too!

Now, more than four thousand take part. They train hard. They show what we can do.

The games began in England in 1948. A doctor named Ludwig Guttmann set up a contest for soldiers who had been hurt in a war. Many could not walk, so they shot arrows from their wheelchairs. In 1960, the first real Paralympic Games were held in Rome, Italy, with about four hundred athletes.

Today, athletes compete in more than twenty sports. Wheelchair basketball is fast and rough. Swimmers race in the pool, and volleyball players compete while they sit on the floor. In goalball, players who cannot see try to roll a ball with bells inside it into a goal. The other team must listen hard to block it.

A blind runner and a guide are joined by a short cord called a tether. They run side by side, and the guide calls out turns. When they win, the guide gets a medal, too.

Now, more than four thousand athletes compete at each Summer Paralympic Games. They come from all over the world, and some come from Saudi Arabia. They train for years, and they show what hard work can do.

MID.prompt: Explain how teamwork and fairness are part of the Paralympic Games. Use at least two details from the article.

MID.modelAnswer: Teamwork is part of the Paralympic Games because a blind runner and a guide are joined by a tether and run side by side, with the guide calling out turns, and when the pair wins, both of them receive a medal. The Games are also made fair and open to everyone, since the name Paralympic comes from the Greek word for beside, showing that the Games run parallel to the Olympics for athletes with many kinds of disabilities, from wheelchair athletes to blind sprinters.

keyWords.definition: a condition in which a part of the body or a sense does not work fully

keyWords.definition: the arranging of people or things into groups based on shared features

keyWords.definition: existing or happening alongside something else in a similar way
keyWords.example: The school runs a parallel program for students who want extra science.

keyWords.definition: describing an artificial body part that replaces a missing one
keyWords.example: After the accident, he learned to walk with a prosthetic leg.

keyWords.definition: the process of helping someone regain health, strength, or skills after an injury or illness
keyWords.example: Swimming was part of her rehabilitation after knee surgery.

HIGH.prompt: Some people think the Olympic and Paralympic Games should be combined into one event. Do you agree or disagree? Support your position with evidence from the article.
checklist: I supported it with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how my evidence supports my position.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I disagree that the Olympic and Paralympic Games should be combined into one event. The article explains that Paralympic sports are specially designed around different disabilities, such as goalball, where players who cannot see use the sound of bells inside the ball, or wheelchair basketball, which depends on the impairment classification of each athlete to keep competition fair. Combining the Games could make it harder to give each sport and classification the attention it deserves, especially since the Paralympic Games already include more than four thousand athletes competing in over twenty sports. Keeping the Games separate, held in the same city just weeks after the Olympics, lets each event celebrate its athletes fully while still showing how closely connected the two competitions are.
